analysis.one_liner: Taxes institutional investors that own single-family homes, forcing them to sell and funding down payment help.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a committee vote, floor vote, or hearing in the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tax any investment vehicle that pools money from investors and buys a single-family house at 50% of the home's value. Entities that already own homes would face a rising tax for each home they keep above a shrinking cap, forcing them to sell off their portfolios over about ten years; hedge funds managing $50 million or more would have to sell all of them. The tax revenue would go into a Housing Downpayment Trust Fund that pays grants to state agencies for down payment help for homebuyers, with priority for families buying homes sold by these investors.
analysis.who_benefits: Families priced out of homeownership, especially first-time buyers competing against corporate buyers making cash offers. The bill channels the tax revenue into down payment grants and pressures investors to sell houses to owner-occupants, with grant priority for buyers of those homes [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: First-time homebuyers competing with investor cash offers

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 50% excise tax on the purchase value of any single-family home (1-4 unit property) acquired by an entity that manages pooled investor funds, making large-scale corporate buying of houses uneconomical [S3].

Requires covered investors to shrink existing portfolios by 10% of their holdings per year for about a decade, down to a floor of 50 homes, and to zero for hedge funds with $50 million or more in assets under management; each home retained above the cap draws a $50,000 annual tax [S3].

Deposits all tax revenue into a Housing Downpayment Trust Fund used for grants to state housing finance agencies for down payment assistance, with priority for families buying homes sold off by covered investors [S2][S3].
Exempts foreclosure properties, owner-occupied homes, and entities primarily engaged in building or rehabilitating homes, aiming the tax at bulk ownership rather than construction [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large investment vehicles that pool outside money and own single-family rental homes, including partnerships, corporations, and REITs, which face the 50% acquisition tax and rising annual taxes on retained homes. Renters could face a tighter rental market in the near term as investor-owned homes are sold rather than rented [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Institutional single-family rental owners and investors

drawbacks.text: The acquisition tax applies to any pooled-investment vehicle buying a home regardless of size, so even small partnerships, community investment funds, or employers housing workers could owe 50% of a home's value [S3].

Selling tens of thousands of rental homes at once could reduce the stock of rental housing in some markets before enough buyers absorb them, and homes sold under the rules cannot go to another business or to anyone who already owns a home, narrowing the buyer pool [S3].

Critics of such proposals argue rents could rise if landlords facing forced divestment raise rents to cover the tax, and that the tax targets symptoms of scarce housing supply rather than building more homes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to prospective first-time buyers is real and direct: money from a tax on investors is converted into down payment help, and corporate owners are pushed to sell to owner-occupants. The costs are transitional and fall on renters and on small pooled-investment vehicles swept in by broad definitions; the 1-to-4 unit definition and the pooled-funds trigger reach well beyond hedge funds despite the bill's name. On balance, the bill targets a concentrated interest and redirects the proceeds to ordinary buyers, but its design would need refinement to avoid hitting small or mission-driven investors.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, never receiving a markup, hearing, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on December 5, 2023, with Sen. Tina Smith as the second sponsor [S1][S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where it stayed for the rest of the 118th Congress [S5][S1].
Only two Democratic senators cosponsored the bill, and no action beyond the referral appears in its legislative history [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Institutional owners of single-family rental homes, which keep their portfolios and face no tax; the largest of these firms hold hundreds of thousands of homes, so even a modest tax rate would have raised billions for down payment assistance.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic sponsors and cosponsors and never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists to show how the parties would have split.

industries.industry: Institutional single-family rental owners (hedge funds, private equity, and REITs in single-family homes)
industries.note: They would owe 50% of the value of any newly bought home and rising annual taxes on retained homes, forcing divestment to owner-occupants. Their business of buying houses and renting them back to would-be buyers competes directly with the families the bill helps.

industries.industry: Asset managers and funds of any size that pool investor money
industries.note: The tax applies to any partnership, corporation, or REIT that manages pooled funds and buys a 1-to-4 unit home, regardless of size, sweeping in small and mission-driven investors alongside hedge funds. The bill's protections cover only nonprofits and builders.

A forced sell-off of investor-owned homes could shrink the rental supply in some markets before buyers absorb them, which could raise rents in the near term. The long-run aim is converting rentals into owner-occupied homes.

industries.industry: First-time homebuyers and state housing finance agencies
industries.note: The bill funds down payment grants through HUD grants to state agencies and gives priority to families buying homes sold by covered investors.
